issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically to stop thinking about a single mugging/robbery is clinically possible but is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile because there are no memory/intrusion items, no trigger-linked re-experiencing pattern, and the formulation leaves Triggers and Memory inactive. This strategy addresses a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the selected items.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but for a mugging/robbery it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The other items emphasize hyperarousal, threat sensitivity, institutional betrayal, and numbing; this culturally/community-focused appraisal is not clearly linked to those features or to the formulation's active appraisal-threat-strategy loop, making it the least coherent appraisal item in this set.

Clinical Vignette: Carmen

Carmen Delgado was fifty-three when she came to the office on a Tuesday afternoon in November, her handbag held tight against her chest even as she sat. She had been a stock broker for twenty-eight years—disciplined, detail-oriented, known in her firm for the steadiness with which she managed client portfolios through market volatility. Her husband, Miguel, had driven her to the appointment. He waited in the lobby, as he had begun to do for most of her outings.

The attack had happened eight months earlier on a warm March evening. Carmen had stayed late at the office to finish a quarterly review, leaving the building around nine o'clock. The parking garage was nearly empty, fluorescent lights casting everything in a sickly yellow. She was two spaces from her car when a man stepped from behind a concrete pillar. He had a knife—she remembered the blade catching the light—and he demanded her purse, her phone, her wedding ring. The encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. He took what he wanted and ran. A security guard found her sitting on the concrete, shaking, ten minutes later. The police came. They took a report. They told her they would investigate. Nothing came of it. The man was never found.

In the weeks after, Carmen had begun to notice how the world had reorganized itself around threat. A car door slamming in her driveway sent electricity through her chest. The sound of Miguel's footsteps behind her in the kitchen made her flinch so violently that once she dropped a plate. She had come to believe that sudden movements—her daughter reaching for something at the dinner table, a colleague gesturing during a meeting—were warnings, little rehearsals of violence. Her body would go rigid, her mind flooded with the image of the blade.

But what had troubled Carmen most deeply was the sense that the people whose job it was to protect her had simply failed. The security guard had not been there when she needed him. The police had taken their report and moved on to other cases. She had paid her taxes, followed the rules, stayed late to do her work well, and the system had let her walk into a parking garage where a man with a knife was waiting. The logic of safety had been exposed as an illusion. The world, she had come to understand with a certainty that felt almost physical, was a dangerous place. Not in the abstract—in the specific, concrete way that meant she could be harmed anywhere, at any moment, by anyone.

She had tried to return to work after two weeks. But sitting at her desk, facing the glass walls of her office, she found herself unable to concentrate. Her eyes kept moving to the doorway. When clients came in, she felt a tightness in her throat. One morning, a colleague had knocked on the glass partition to ask a question, and Carmen had gasped so loudly that others turned to stare. She had taken medical leave.

At home, she had developed small rituals. Before going to bed, she would visualize the day in reverse, mentally rehearsing safety at each moment—a way of convincing herself, she supposed, that if she could see it all again and find no danger, then perhaps the next day would be safe too. She performed these visualizations every night, sometimes for an hour or more. She also found herself becoming intensely agreeable with Miguel, with her daughter, with anyone who approached her with even a hint of irritation. If someone seemed upset, she would immediately defer, apologize, do whatever was needed to smooth the moment. The thought that someone might become angry with her, that a moment of conflict might escalate into something dangerous, was unbearable.

She had stopped going to the parking garage altogether. She no longer went out after dark. She asked Miguel to accompany her to the grocery store, to the bank, to her own medical appointments. At work, even on medical leave, she had begun scanning the firm's security protocols obsessively, checking the email updates about access cards and camera placements, as if understanding the system's architecture might somehow prevent another failure.

What had finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her supervisor. The firm wanted to know when she would return. Her medical leave was running out. Carmen realized, with a hollow kind of clarity, that she could not imagine going back to that parking garage, to that office, to the life she had built. She felt dead inside when she thought about it—not sad, but absent, as though the part of her that had cared about her career, her independence, her place in the world had been taken along with her purse that night. She was terrified of what would happen if she did return, and equally terrified of what would happen if she did not.
